name: Uniform distribution
seoTitle: Uniform distribution Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: Uniform distribution: work out mean from the parameter and the quantile. A free statistics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Uniform distribution calculator the parameter and the quantile and it returns mean. That makes it useful for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. Change one value and the results step aside until you press Calculate again, which is what makes it easy to see how much the answer really depends on that one input.

sections.title: How does the Uniform distribution calculator work?
sections.html:
The Uniform distribution calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports mean in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the mode and the probability type); then you type in the parameter (a), the parameter (b), the quantile (p) and the sample length.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: The formula behind the Uniform distribution calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Mean=((1 ÷ 2) × parameter (a) + (1 ÷ 2) × parameter (b))
Variance=((1 ÷ 12) × (parameter (a) ^ 2) − 1 ÷ 6 × parameter (a) × parameter (b) + (1 ÷ 12) × (parameter (b) ^ 2))
Median=((1 ÷ 2) × parameter (a) + (1 ÷ 2) × parameter (b))
P(X ≤ x)=(X, parameter (a), parameter (b))
P(X < x)=(X, parameter (a), parameter (b))
P(X ≥ x)=1 − (X, parameter (a), parameter (b))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Uniform distribution calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the parameter and the quantile — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Uniform distribution calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns mean, derived from the parameter and the quantile. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Uniform distribution calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the parameter and the quantile, which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Mean = 0.5. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Uniform distribution calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
